So a quasi-complete H is **not** quasi-perfect iff either:
- **(a)** H has no transversal (Hall's condition fails), or
- **(b)** |H| = n and H is itself a transversal (no proper subset of size n exists).

## Finding ϑ(n): Maximum size of quasi-complete, non-quasi-perfect sets

**Case (b)** gives max size n. **Case (a)** requires a Hall violation: ∃ row-set S with |S| = s, |N(S)| = t < s. Edges from S go only to N(S) (≤ s·t), edges from non-S rows go anywhere (≤ (n−s)·n). So:

|H| ≤ s·t + (n−s)·n = n² + s(t−n)

With constraints 2 ≤ s ≤ n−1, 1 ≤ t ≤ s−1. Since t ≤ s−1:

s(t−n) ≤ s(s−1−n) = s² − (n+1)s

This quadratic in s opens upward, so on [2, n−1] its maximum is at the endpoints: h(2) = h(n−1) = 2−2n. Therefore:

|H| ≤ n² + (2−2n) = (n−1)² + 1

This maximum is achieved at **(s,t) = (n−1, n−2)** or **(s,t) = (2, 1)**, with all cells filled. For n ≥ 3, (n−1)²+1 > n, so case (a) dominates. Thus:

**ϑ(n) = (n−1)² + 2**, giving **ϑ(20) = 19² + 2 = 363**.

## Finding ρ(n): Counting extremal non-quasi-perfect sets

We count quasi-complete, non-quasi-perfect sets of size (n−1)²+1. For n ≥ 3, size > n so only case (a) applies. Any such set must achieve the maximum, meaning s(t−n) = −2n+2, forcing (s,t) ∈ {(n−1, n−2), (2,1)} with all cells filled.

## Setup and Key Definitions

A set H is **quasi-complete** if every row and column has ≥1 cell in H. A set K is **quasi-perfect** if it contains a transversal (n cells, one per row, one per column) as a **proper** subset, requiring both a transversal and |K| > n.

So a quasi-complete H is **not** quasi-perfect iff either:
- **(a)** H has no transversal (Hall's condition fails), or
- **(b)** |H| = n and H is itself a transversal (no proper subset of size n exists).

## Finding ϑ(n): Maximum size of quasi-complete, non-quasi-perfect sets

|H| ≤ s·t + (n−s)·n = n² + s(t−n)

With constraints 2 ≤ s ≤ n−1, 1 ≤ t ≤ s−1. Since t ≤ s−1:

s(t−n) ≤ s(s−1−n) = s² − (n+1)s

This quadratic in s opens upward, so on [2, n−1] its maximum is at the endpoints: h(2) = h(n−1) = 2−2n. Therefore:

|H| ≤ n² + (2−2n) = (n−1)² + 1

This maximum is achieved at **(s,t) = (n−1, n−2)** or **(s,t) = (2, 1)**, with all cells filled. For n ≥ 3, (n−1)²+1 > n, so case (a) dominates. Thus:
